questions.knowledge_point: Using Radioactive Dating to Estimate the Age of an Object
questions.problem: At a geological site, a sample of a lunar rock is found with $84%$ of its original rubidium-87 content. Given that the half-life of rubidium-87 is $49.72$ billion years, approximately how old is the sample?
questions.worked_solution:
The mass $M(t)$ of a radioactive substance at time $t$ can be modeled by the differential equation

$$
{M}^{′}(t)=-kM(t),\,M(0)={M}_{0}.
$$

The general solution to this equation is

$$
M(t)={M}_{0}{e}^{-kt}.
$$

The half-life ${t}_{1/2}$ is the time taken for the mass of the substance to reduce by one half and is given by

$$
{t}_{1/2}=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{k}.
$$

Since we know that ${t}_{1/2}=49.72$ billion years, we have

$$
49.72=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{k}\,⇒\,k=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{49.72}.
$$

So, we have

$$
M(t)={M}_{0}{e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/49.72}.
$$

We wish to calculate the time $t$ such that $M(t)=0.84{M}_{0}.$ So, we set up our equation as follows:

$$
0.84{M}_{0}={M}_{0}{e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/49.72}
$$

Solving this equation for $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}0.84{M}_{0} & ={M}_{0}{e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/49.72} \\ 0.84\cancel{{M}_{0}} & =\cancel{{M}_{0}}{e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/49.72} \\ 0.84 & ={e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/49.72} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(0.84) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/49.72}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(0.84) & =-\frac{t\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{49.72} \\ t & =-\frac{49.72\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(0.84)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\ t & ≈12.5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the sample is approximately $12.5$ billion years old.

questions.problem: Samarium-147 has a half-life of $106.1$ billion years. A sample of samarium-147 has an initial mass of $300\,\mu \text{g}.$ Rounded to the nearest integer, what is the mass of the sample after $80$ billion years?
questions.worked_solution:
The mass $M(t)$ of a radioactive substance at time $t$ can be modeled by the differential equation

$$
{M}^{′}(t)=-kM(t),\,M(0)={M}_{0}.
$$

The general solution to this equation is

$$
M(t)={M}_{0}{e}^{-kt}.
$$

The half-life ${t}_{1/2}$ is the time taken for the mass of the substance to reduce by one half and is given by

$$
{t}_{1/2}=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{k}.
$$

Since we know that ${t}_{1/2}=106.1$ billion years, we have

$$
106.1=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{k}\,⇒\,k=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{106.1}.
$$

Also, since ${M}_{0}=300\,\mu \text{g},$ we have the particular solution

$$
M(t)=300{e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/106.1}.
$$

Finally,

$$
M(80)=300{e}^{-80\operatorname{ln}⁡2/106.1}≈178
$$

rounded to the nearest integer. 

Therefore, we conclude that there will be $178\,\mu \text{g}$ of the sample left.

questions.problem:
The half-life of cobalt-60 is $5.27$ years. How long does it take for a $8.0\,\mu \text{g}$ sample of cobalt-60 to reduce to $0.5\,\mu \text{g}?$ Do not round the answer.

$t=$
{{field-1}}
$\text{yr}$
questions.worked_solution:
The mass $M(t)$ of a radioactive substance at time $t$ can be modeled by the differential equation

$$
{M}^{′}(t)=-kM(t),\,M(0)={M}_{0}.
$$

The general solution to this equation is

$$
M(t)={M}_{0}{e}^{-kt}.
$$

The half-life ${t}_{1/2}$ is the time taken for the mass of the substance to reduce by one half and is given by

$$
{t}_{1/2}=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{k}.
$$

There are two methods that we can use to solve this problem. We describe each of them below.

**Method 1**

Since we know that ${t}_{1/2}=5.27$ years, we have

$$
5.27=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{k}\,⇒\,k=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{5.27}
$$

Also, since ${M}_{0}=8.0\,\mu \text{g},$ we have the particular solution

$$
M(t)=8.0{e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/5.27}.
$$

We wish to calculate the time $t$ such that $M(t)=0.5\,\mu \text{g}.$ So, we set up our equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}0.5 & =8.0{e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/5.27}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this equation for $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}0.5 & =8.0{e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/5.27} \\ \frac{0.5}{8.0} & ={e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/5.27} \\ \frac{1}{16} & ={e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/5.27} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{16}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/5.27}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡1-\operatorname{ln}⁡16 & =-\frac{t\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{5.27} \\ -\operatorname{ln}⁡16 & =-\frac{t\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{5.27} \\ t & =\frac{5.27\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡16}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\ t & =\frac{5.27\cdot 4\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\ t & =21.08\,\text{yr}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Method 2**

We wish to calculate the time $t$ such that $M(t)=0.5\,\mu \text{g}.$ Notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{M(t)}{M(0)} & =\frac{0.5\,\mu \text{g}}{8.0\,\mu \text{g}} \\  & =\frac{1}{16} \\  & ={(\frac{1}{2})}^{4},\end{aligned}
$$

or equivalently

$$
M(t)={(\frac{1}{2})}^{4}\cdot M(0).
$$

From this equation, we see that $4$ half-lives must have occurred for the mass to reduce from $8.0\,\mu \text{g}$ to $0.5\,\mu \text{g}.$ Hence,

$$
t=4\cdot {t}_{1/2}=4\cdot 5.27=21.08\,\text{yr}.
$$

questions.problem:
The half-life of fluorine-18 is $109.7$ minutes. How long does it take for a $6.4\,\text{ng}$ sample of fluorine-18 to reduce to $0.2\,\text{ng}?$ Do not round the answer.

$t=$
{{field-1}}
$\text{min}$
questions.worked_solution:
The mass $M(t)$ of a radioactive substance at time $t$ can be modeled by the differential equation

$$
{M}^{′}(t)=-kM(t),\,M(0)={M}_{0}.
$$

The general solution to this equation is

$$
M(t)={M}_{0}{e}^{-kt}.
$$

The half-life ${t}_{1/2}$ is the time taken for the mass of the substance to reduce by one half and is given by

$$
{t}_{1/2}=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{k}.
$$

There are two methods that we can use to solve this problem. We describe each of them below.

**Method 1**

Since we know that ${t}_{1/2}=109.7$ minutes, we have

$$
109.7=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{k}\,⇒\,k=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{109.7}
$$

Also, since ${M}_{0}=6.4\,\text{ng},$ we have the particular solution

$$
M(t)=6.4{e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/109.7}.
$$

We wish to calculate the time $t$ such that $M(t)=0.2\,\text{ng}.$ So, we set up our equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}0.2 & =6.4{e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/109.7}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this equation for $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}0.2 & =6.4{e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/109.7} \\ \frac{0.2}{6.4} & ={e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/109.7} \\ \frac{1}{32} & ={e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/109.7} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{32}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/109.7}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡1-\operatorname{ln}⁡32 & =-\frac{t\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{109.7} \\ -\operatorname{ln}⁡32 & =-\frac{t\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{109.7} \\ t & =\frac{109.7\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡32}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\ t & =\frac{109.7\cdot 5\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\ t & =548.5\,\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Method 2**

We wish to calculate the time $t$ such that $M(t)=0.2\,\text{ng}.$ Notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{M(t)}{M(0)} & =\frac{0.2\,\text{ng}}{6.4\,\text{ng}} \\  & =\frac{1}{32} \\  & ={(\frac{1}{2})}^{5},\end{aligned}
$$

or equivalently

$$
M(t)={(\frac{1}{2})}^{5}\cdot M(0).
$$

From this equation, we see that $5$ half-lives must have occurred for the mass to reduce from $6.4\,\text{ng}$ to $0.2\,\text{ng}.$ Hence,

$$
t=5\cdot {t}_{1/2}=5\cdot 109.7=548.5\,\text{min}.
$$

$$

$$

$$

So, we have

$$
M(t)={M}_{0}{e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/1.39}.

$$
